user_message: Help me answer a job interview question about a time I improved a process.

cards.Situation: New engineers on my team took about six weeks to ship their first production change, and two of the four hires that year said onboarding was the reason they nearly left.
cards.Task: I owned making onboarding faster without adding headcount to the platform team.
cards.Action: I interviewed every recent hire, mapped where they got stuck, replaced the wiki with a runnable setup script, and paired each new engineer with a rotating owner for their first two weeks.
cards.Result: First production change dropped from six weeks to under two weeks, and the next four hires all shipped in their first fortnight.

recorded_draft:
When I joined the platform team, onboarding was a mess. According to Gartner, poor onboarding costs organisations 30% of first-year productivity, and studies show that engineers who ship early stay longer.

I owned fixing it. I interviewed recent hires, mapped the blockers, replaced the wiki with a runnable setup script, and paired each new engineer with a rotating owner.

The result was a 47% reduction in time-to-first-commit and an estimated $1,200,000 in retained productivity across the org.
recorded_regenerations:
When I joined the platform team, new engineers took about six weeks to ship their first production change, and two of the four hires that year told me onboarding was the reason they nearly left.

I owned making onboarding faster without adding headcount. I interviewed every recent hire, mapped where they got stuck, replaced the wiki with a runnable setup script, and paired each new engineer with a rotating owner for their first two weeks.

Time to first production change dropped from six weeks to under two weeks, and the next four hires all shipped in their first fortnight. What I would repeat is starting from the interviews rather than from my own guess about what was slow.
